title: Ethical Hacking: Authorized Lab Assessment and Remediation Verification

stageOutcomes.outcome: Scope an authorized assessment and map a resettable isolated lab using Linux, network and HTTP evidence.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Rules of engagement, verified loopback/host-only containment, a synthetic asset/request map and a baseline evidence log.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Validate bounded local input, file, identity, access-control and browser-boundary weaknesses without collecting real data.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Reproducible lab findings with positive/negative controls, minimal harmless proof and documented restoration.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Assess API/server-request and local infrastructure boundaries, challenge tool output and prioritize defensible findings.
stageOutcomes.evidence: An API boundary matrix, offline container/configuration review and independently reproducible, context-rated findings.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Run an authorized assessment lifecycle from planning through reporting, remediation, retesting and handover.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A scoped local-lab capstone report, owner-approved fixes, before/after regression evidence and a responsible-disclosure tabletop.

resources.title: PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Getting started
resources.notes: Reading is public and free. Optional hosted labs may require a free Academy account and must stay within that lab's authorization. The required route uses owned local fixtures; Burp Professional and certification are not required.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG v4.2: The OWASP Testing Framework
resources.license: Official versioned guide; linked, not reproduced
resources.notes: Direct versioned v4.2 chapter body, not only its index; avoids the currently broken stable-site redirect. Use SDLC and maintenance/retest phases, following its Introduction cross-reference for balanced testing. Complement historical examples with current guidance and explicit lab authorization.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Web Application Security Testing
resources.notes: Verified directories include Information Gathering, Configuration, Identity, Authentication, Authorization, Sessions, Input Validation, Client-side and API Testing. Read the named category; this curriculum never authorizes testing any non-lab target.

resources.title: OWASP WSTG v4.2: Reporting
resources.notes: Use report structure, executive communication and reproducible technical evidence. Assignments are original; do not republish copied WSTG text or disclose actual third-party vulnerabilities.

resources.title: OWASP Juice Shop: official repository and local setup
resources.license: Official project instructions; no app content rehosted
resources.notes: Deliberately vulnerable training software. Use a pinned official release only in a disposable owned lab, with loopback/host-only binding and synthetic data. Never use its shared public demo as an assessment target or expose a local instance to a LAN/Internet. A source-runtime route is available without paid container software.

resources.title: OWASP WebGoat: official warnings and local installation
resources.notes: The README explicitly warns against unauthorized testing and recommends disconnection/isolation; examples bind to 127.0.0.1. Use only local dummy accounts. Check the chosen release's Java/runtime requirements; no public instance, external victim or paid lab is required.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: SQL injection
resources.notes: Read the data/query boundary, detection limitations and prevention sections. Practice uses benign synthetic records and local instrumentation only; no credential extraction, schema dumping, destructive statements or external targets.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: Path traversal
resources.notes: Read root-containment failures and prevention. The only file proof allowed here is a deliberately created harmless marker in a disposable lab, never OS secrets, private files or a real host mount.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: Access control
resources.notes: Use horizontal/vertical access-control and insecure direct object reference concepts with exactly two synthetic owners in a local fixture. Never enumerate real users or extract real records.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: Authentication
resources.notes: Read authentication, session and recovery failure classes. The assigned method is bounded state-transition testing with known dummy accounts, not password guessing, credential stuffing, phishing or real identity collection.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: Cross-site scripting
resources.notes: Study reflected/stored/DOM contexts and context-sensitive defenses. Use inert markers or the owned lab's harmless built-in indicator only; no cookie reads, exfiltration, external callbacks or persistent client modifications.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: Cross-site request forgery
resources.notes: Read conditions and defenses for unintended authenticated actions. Local tests may change only a disposable note or preference using the learner's dummy identity; no real user is induced to visit anything.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: Cross-origin resource sharing
resources.notes: Compare origin policy, response sharing and credential assumptions. Test only explicitly owned lab origins; CORS is not a substitute for server-side authorization.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: API testing
resources.notes: Read API documentation, endpoints, supported methods and mass-assignment concepts. Use a predeclared local request inventory and bounded synthetic cases; do not probe unknown public APIs or cause resource exhaustion.

resources.title: PortSwigger Academy: Server-side request forgery
resources.notes: Understand delegated server authority and destination validation. Exercises use two explicitly owned local HTTP sinks only: no cloud metadata endpoint, private-network discovery, external callback, credential collection or protocol exploitation.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-115: Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
resources.license: Official US government publication; link-only here
resources.notes: September 2008 historical assessment-process reference. Use planning, rules of engagement, execution control and post-assessment reporting; do not treat its tool/protocol details as current configuration or legal advice.

resources.title: Optional PortSwigger Academy learning paths
resources.license: Provider-hosted practice under its terms; link-only
resources.notes: Optional hosted practice may require a free account. Authorization applies only to your assigned lab instance and its rules, not the provider's infrastructure or other sites. All required original assignments have a local-only route.

resources.title: Optional CMU CyLab Security Academy
resources.license: Provider-hosted practice under its terms; link-only
resources.notes: Current home of the migrated picoCTF learning platform, verified from picoCTF's official notice and this landing page. Optional account-required General Skills/Web practice only within assigned challenge authorization; no stale picoCTF practice links or requirement to pursue other categories.

modules.title: 01. Authorization, isolation and evidence discipline
modules.description: Begin an assessment only when ownership, boundaries, harmless proof and reset procedures are explicit.

lessons.title: Write scope and rules of engagement before testing
objectives: Distinguish permission to read a site from authorization to assess it.
Define targets, allowed methods, data handling, time windows and stop conditions.

topics.title: Authority
details: A public endpoint, employer relationship or bug-bounty label is not blanket permission.
Written scope identifies the owner, exact assets and permitted actions.

topics.title: Bounded testing
details: Minimize proof and avoid affecting availability or other users.
Unexpected real data or an out-of-scope destination requires stopping.

reading.locator: Planning and post-assessment portions of the official SP 800-115 publication, including rules-of-engagement guidance; use process concepts, not historical tool recommendations.

assignment.title: A fictional assessment authorization pack
instructions: Act as owner and assessor of a fictional local notes application; identify the exact loopback/host-only endpoints and synthetic accounts.
Write allowed request types, a small request budget, excluded actions, evidence retention and a stop/escalation procedure.
Evaluate three scope changes: a redirect outside the lab, unexpected real data and a request to test a coworker's account. Do not perform them.
acceptanceCriteria: Only owned/expressly authorized isolated assets are in scope.
No real credentials, private records, availability disruption or external target testing is permitted.
Stop conditions and the person/role authorized to expand scope are explicit.

questions.prompt: A lab response redirects to an unrelated public host. What should the assessor do?
choices: Stop following that path and seek scope clarification
Continue because the first request was authorized
Scan the new host automatically
questions.answer: Stop following that path and seek scope clarification
questions.explanation: Authorization does not automatically transfer through a redirect. The exact destination and permitted actions must remain within the engagement boundary.

questions.prompt: Why include stop conditions rather than only a target list?
questions.answer: Unexpected data, impact or destinations can make a previously safe action out of scope; stop rules define how to contain that uncertainty without improvising permission.
questions.explanation: Authorization is an operational constraint throughout testing, not a one-time checkbox.

reviewPrompts: What evidence establishes permission for this exact action?

lessons.title: Create and verify a resettable deliberately vulnerable lab
objectives: Choose an official training target without exposing it to a shared network.
Verify binding, egress restrictions, synthetic data and reset behavior.

topics.title: Lab containment
details: Deliberately vulnerable applications must not bind publicly or mount host secrets.
Loopback publication and a disposable host-only VM are different but bounded designs.

topics.title: Repeatability
details: Pin the target release and record the runtime.
A reset must restore expected dummy accounts, data and application state.

reading.locator: README warnings and Installation instructions: localhost defaults and explicit 127.0.0.1 port bindings. Check the selected release's runtime requirements rather than copying an old version string.

assignment.title: A contained training-target baseline
instructions: Choose one official local WebGoat or Juice Shop release in a disposable owned VM or a minimal locally authored vulnerable fixture; no public demo is a target.
Bind only to loopback or the approved host-only segment, deny unneeded egress, use disposable dummy accounts and mount no host/user directories.
Verify listening addresses, make one harmless local page request, save a baseline and prove a reset. Record the exact target/runtime versions and teardown steps.
acceptanceCriteria: The target is not reachable through an unintended LAN/Internet-facing binding.
There are no real secrets, personal data or production mounts.
Reset restores the declared synthetic fixture; unsafe exposure causes testing to stop.

questions.prompt: Which target is appropriate for the required assessment route?
choices: The project's shared public demo
Any site built with the same framework
A pinned official training app in your isolated local lab
questions.answer: A pinned official training app in your isolated local lab
questions.explanation: A software project being intentionally vulnerable does not authorize attacks on every hosted instance. Control and scope must be explicit.

questions.prompt: Why avoid mounting a home directory into a deliberately vulnerable container?
questions.answer: A lab flaw could then reach real files or credentials outside the synthetic exercise, breaking the containment boundary.
questions.explanation: Isolation depends on mounts and permissions as well as network bindings.

reviewPrompts: Could a mistake in the training app affect anything outside the disposable lab?

lessons.title: Capture minimal, reproducible evidence without secrets
objectives: Distinguish an observation, a hypothesis and a confirmed finding.
Record target version, request context, expected/actual behavior and restoration.

topics.title: Evidence discipline
details: The smallest harmless proof is preferable to collecting more data.
Redact session values and preserve test IDs, timestamps and causal context.

topics.title: Finding quality
details: A tool alert is a lead rather than a verdict.
Negative controls and reproducibility reduce false conclusions.

reading.locator: Reporting README: report components and technical finding communication. Build an original finding record rather than copying a report template verbatim.

assignment.title: A redacted evidence notebook
instructions: Record a benign local request and an expected denial from your lab with method, path, synthetic role, time, target version and response status.
Create a hypothesis for an unexpected result and state a bounded confirming test and a negative control.
Replace all dummy session values with redacted placeholders and define evidence access, retention and deletion rules.
acceptanceCriteria: A reviewer can repeat the action using newly issued dummy sessions without seeing secret values.
Facts and unconfirmed interpretations are labelled separately.
Proof stops after the minimum synthetic result needed to demonstrate the issue.

questions.prompt: Which is a confirmed-finding record rather than just a lead?
choices: A scoped reproducible boundary violation with expected/actual results and controls
A scanner's severity label alone
A screenshot with no target version or context
questions.answer: A scoped reproducible boundary violation with expected/actual results and controls
questions.explanation: Confirmation needs evidence that the intended boundary actually failed under stated conditions, not just a tool's interpretation.

questions.prompt: Why redact even disposable session tokens from a shared report?
questions.answer: It builds correct evidence-handling discipline and avoids distributing reusable authority while preserving the context needed to reproduce the test.
questions.explanation: A report should explain how to obtain a test session, not circulate the original credential.

reviewPrompts: What is the least data needed to prove this claim?

modules.title: 02. Linux, network and HTTP assessment foundations
modules.description: Map only the assets you own and understand normal behavior before interpreting a failure.

lessons.title: Inspect lab processes, permissions and service exposure
objectives: Relate processes, users, files and listening endpoints.
Identify unnecessary lab exposure without broad scanning or privilege escalation.

topics.title: Host context
details: A process's user and permissions bound its authority.
A listening address reveals intended reachability, not the whole application policy.

topics.title: Safe inventory
details: Read the owned lab's service/configuration inventory before testing.
Do not enumerate external ranges, host secrets or other users' files.

video.locator: Week 2 Securing Systems: ports, firewalls and service boundaries. This exercise uses read-only local inventory rather than public scanning.

reading.locator: 02-Configuration_and_Deployment_Management_Testing: infrastructure and application configuration review. Apply only to the known local target and its declared ports.

assignment.title: An owned-lab exposure inventory
instructions: Inside the disposable lab, record process identity, executable/version, known listening address/port and synthetic data directory permissions.
Compare the inventory with the rules of engagement, flagging one unnecessary capability or documenting why none is present.
Verify a harmless connection to one declared endpoint and a denied synthetic-file access; perform no network-range scan or privilege escalation.
deliverables: Scope comparison and bounded observation log
acceptanceCriteria: All observations concern declared lab assets only.
Process identity and application user identity are not confused.
Unnecessary exposure is treated as a finding to review, not permission to explore beyond scope.

questions.prompt: A service unexpectedly listens on all interfaces. What does the assessor do first?
choices: Invite external users to test it
Assume the lab is safe because the app is educational
Stop and correct or escalate the containment issue
questions.answer: Stop and correct or escalate the containment issue
questions.explanation: The target's reachability may now exceed authorization and expose a deliberately vulnerable service. Containment takes priority over assessment progress.

questions.prompt: Why record the process user as well as the signed-in application user?
questions.answer: They represent different authority boundaries: one governs OS resources and the other governs application permissions.
questions.explanation: A weakness's impact depends on both layers of authority.

reviewPrompts: Which unexpected capability expands the possible impact of a lab flaw?

lessons.title: Trace HTTP methods, parameters, cookies and responses
objectives: Read a normal request/response and identify state and trust boundaries.
Use browser developer tools or a scoped local proxy without affecting unrelated browsing.

topics.title: HTTP contract
details: Method, path, headers, body and status each carry different meaning.
Client fields are not authoritative simply because the UI produced them.

topics.title: Tool hygiene
details: Restrict interception/history to the owned target.
Use an isolated browser profile; never install a test CA in the host-wide store.

video.locator: Week 3 Securing Software: developer tools, requests and client/server validation. Observe the local app's benign normal behavior first.

reading.locator: API reconnaissance and API documentation: identify methods, paths, parameters and response shapes from the local target's own normal traffic and documentation.

assignment.title: A normal-flow request notebook
instructions: Capture the local dummy user's sign-in, note read, note update and sign-out using an isolated browser profile and developer tools.
Annotate method, path, content type, state-changing fields, cookie presence and response code without retaining token values.
If using a free intercepting proxy, restrict it to the exact local origin and show that unrelated browsing is excluded; developer tools alone satisfy the assignment.
acceptanceCriteria: The notebook distinguishes expected state changes from reads.
No real browsing session or non-lab traffic is captured.
No client owner/role field is assumed to be trustworthy without a server check.

questions.prompt: A role field appears in a browser request. What does its presence establish?
choices: Only that the client supplied the field
That the server should trust the role
That the caller has administrative authority
questions.answer: Only that the client supplied the field
questions.explanation: The authoritative service must establish permissions independently. Observing a field is not evidence that it is trusted or exploitable.

questions.prompt: Why use a separate browser profile for lab interception?
questions.answer: It prevents unrelated sessions, cookies and browsing data from entering the tool's history or trust configuration.
questions.explanation: Tool setup is itself a privacy and scope boundary.

reviewPrompts: Which fields describe intent, and which component decides authority?

lessons.title: Build a bounded asset and authorization baseline
objectives: Map known endpoints, actors and intended permissions.
Choose tests by trust boundary instead of spraying generic probes.

topics.title: Assessment map
details: Record how each endpoint was discovered within normal authorized use.
Unknown or redirected assets remain out of scope until explicitly included.

topics.title: Baseline controls
details: Expected denials establish useful negative controls.
Test selection should follow threats, impact and the request budget.

reading.locator: 01-Information_Gathering and 05-Authorization_Testing: map entry points, execution paths and intended authorization in the owned lab only.

assignment.title: Beginner evidence gate: a scoped test inventory
instructions: Combine the local service inventory and normal HTTP traces into a map of endpoints, data stores and synthetic roles.
Define owner, other-owner and anonymous expectations for each selected operation.
Choose a small prioritized set of tests with proof limits, negative controls, reset steps and explicit stop conditions.
deliverables: Prioritized bounded test plan and baseline checks
acceptanceCriteria: Every planned request has a known authorized destination and purpose.
Expected allowed and denied behaviors are written before testing.
The plan includes reset/evidence handling and excludes unknown targets and unbounded scans.

questions.prompt: What should drive test selection after mapping a small lab?
choices: The largest possible request count
A list of unrelated public hosts
Its trust boundaries and authorized risk questions
questions.answer: Its trust boundaries and authorized risk questions
questions.explanation: A focused assessment gathers evidence about the system's actual assumptions while minimizing unnecessary impact.

questions.prompt: Why state expected behavior before sending a test?
questions.answer: It makes a failure distinguishable from normal behavior and prevents interpreting any unusual response as a vulnerability.
questions.explanation: A clear control expectation is necessary for an evidence-based finding.

reviewPrompts: Which test has the highest information value for the least possible impact?

modules.title: 03. Input interpretation and file boundaries
modules.description: Validate local data/control separation using harmless fixtures and explicit negative controls.

lessons.title: Validate an injection hypothesis without extracting data
objectives: Trace untrusted input to query interpretation in a deliberately vulnerable local example.
Distinguish an error symptom from a confirmed data/control boundary failure.

topics.title: Injection mechanism
details: Concatenating data into query syntax can change interpretation.
A quoted surname causing an error is a clue, not proof of exploitable injection.

topics.title: Bounded proof
details: Use synthetic records and local query instrumentation, never credential tables or data dumps.
A parameterized version provides a negative control and remediation target.

video.locator: Week 3 Securing Software: SQL injection and prepared statements. Focus on the mechanism and defensive comparison, not external exploitation.

reading.locator: What is SQL injection?, detecting SQL injection, and prevention using parameterized queries. Restrict proof to the instrumented synthetic fixture.

assignment.title: A query-boundary finding with a safe control
instructions: Use a local teaching fixture with three invented product records and visible query-construction logging, or an explicitly assigned local training lesson.
Compare ordinary text and a benign quote-containing name; inspect whether data enter query syntax and use the local lesson's minimal harmless indicator to validate the hypothesis.
Compare a parameterized variant, documenting expected/actual behavior. Do not enumerate schemas, extract credentials, execute destructive statements or contact another target.
deliverables: Redacted local finding and mechanism explanation
acceptanceCriteria: An error alone is not labelled confirmed injection.
Proof demonstrates the input-to-query boundary using only synthetic fixture data.
The parameterized control preserves legitimate quoted input and prevents syntax interpretation.

questions.prompt: A quote in a search field causes a server error. What has been established?
choices: A diagnostic lead needing scoped confirmation
Permission to dump a database
Certain proof of every form of SQL injection
questions.answer: A diagnostic lead needing scoped confirmation
questions.explanation: Errors can have many causes. A finding requires evidence of the relevant interpretation boundary and a bounded authorized proof.

questions.prompt: Why include legitimate quote-containing text in remediation tests?
questions.answer: The fix should keep user input as data without breaking valid names or content; simply banning characters is not a complete query-construction defense.
questions.explanation: Security and functional correctness should be verified together.

reviewPrompts: What observation confirms the mechanism rather than merely a symptom?

lessons.title: Assess path containment and upload assumptions
objectives: Test whether a local file interface enforces an allowed root.
Separate filename, media type, content validation and storage permissions.

topics.title: Path interpretation
details: Normalization and containment are different checks.
A file outside an application's allowed root can still be inside the disposable lab proof boundary.

topics.title: Upload handling
details: Extensions and client-declared content types are untrusted metadata.
Storage should not grant uploaded content execution authority.

reading.locator: File path traversal concepts and prevention: resolve and enforce the allowed root; do not use example sensitive OS files as test targets.

assignment.title: A harmless file-boundary assessment
instructions: Create an allowed document folder and a separate harmless marker folder within the disposable fixture; neither may contain real host data.
Test normal, normalized and out-of-root requests against a local teaching endpoint, stopping after a single marker proves the boundary behavior.
For uploads, use only plain text with conflicting extension/type metadata; compare acceptance, storage location and non-executable handling before/after a fix.
deliverables: Allowed-root diagram and bounded test table
acceptanceCriteria: No real filesystem, secret, executable payload or host-mounted file is read or uploaded.
The finding distinguishes normalization from enforceable containment.
The fixed path rejects out-of-root access while preserving legitimate documents.

questions.prompt: Normalizing a user-supplied path is sufficient only if what also happens?
choices: The user picked a friendly filename
The resolved target is checked against the authorized root and policy
The file extension is short
questions.answer: The resolved target is checked against the authorized root and policy
questions.explanation: Normalization produces a canonical interpretation; it does not decide whether that location is permitted.

questions.prompt: Why is a plain-text marker preferable to reading a system secret as proof?
questions.answer: It demonstrates the same access boundary failure with minimal impact and without collecting sensitive data or expanding scope.
questions.explanation: An ethical assessment proves the relevant condition, not the maximum possible harm.

reviewPrompts: Does the test prove the boundary while leaving all real data untouched?

modules.title: 04. Identity, access-control and session assessment
modules.description: Use known dummy identities to test authority transitions and owner boundaries.

lessons.title: Validate horizontal and vertical access-control failures
objectives: Compare intended and observed permissions for synthetic owners and roles.
Confirm an ownership flaw with one minimal local record, not enumeration.

topics.title: Access failure classes
details: Horizontal failures cross owners; vertical failures cross privilege levels.
Predictable IDs do not themselves prove unauthorized access.

topics.title: Confirmation
details: Control requests establish what each known actor should see.
Lists, reads and writes can fail independently.

reading.locator: Horizontal and vertical privilege escalation, insecure direct object references and access-control prevention. Apply only to the two predeclared synthetic users.

assignment.title: A two-user ownership proof
instructions: Prepare Alice/Bob dummy records and a narrowly scoped synthetic support role in a deliberately vulnerable local fixture.
Compare authorized self-access with one known other-owner read and one reversible update; restore the fixture immediately.
Record a local list/role boundary separately, stopping at the first minimal proof and never guessing or enumerating real identifiers.
deliverables: Minimal finding record and restoration log
acceptanceCriteria: The report identifies principal, action, resource and violated policy.
Only predeclared synthetic IDs and reversible fixture changes are used.
Predictability of an ID is not substituted for proof of unauthorized access.

questions.prompt: Sequential record IDs by themselves establish what?
choices: A confirmed cross-user data leak
An identifier pattern, not necessarily an authorization flaw
Permission to enumerate the service
questions.answer: An identifier pattern, not necessarily an authorization flaw
questions.explanation: Access control may still be correct. The relevant finding is an unauthorized operation succeeding under a scoped test.

questions.prompt: What is a useful negative control for a cross-owner read test?
questions.answer: A request by the rightful owner that should succeed, paired with an anonymous or other-owner request that should be denied under the declared policy.
questions.explanation: Controls distinguish authorization behavior from a missing record, application error or misunderstood workflow.

reviewPrompts: Which exact permission check is absent or incorrect?

lessons.title: Test login, logout, recovery and session transitions safely
objectives: Evaluate authority before and after a session-state change.
Identify recovery and token-validation assumptions without guessing credentials.

topics.title: State transitions
details: Logout and role changes must affect the right sessions.
Client deletion alone may leave server authority active.

topics.title: Authentication scope
details: Known dummy credentials are sufficient to test session lifecycle.
Password spraying, real MFA interception and credential collection are outside this curriculum.

video.locator: Week 0 Securing Accounts: authentication, MFA and recovery concepts. Use current NIST guidance for requirements and bounded dummy-session tests for evidence.

reading.locator: Authentication mechanisms and vulnerabilities in other authentication mechanisms; use these as a checklist for explicit local lifecycle transitions, not password attacks.

assignment.title: A dummy-session transition matrix
instructions: With one known dummy account, record successful login and a permitted operation, then logout, expire or revoke the session using local controls.
Attempt only the same benign operation after each transition, keeping token values out of evidence.
Review the fictional recovery flow on paper for assurance gaps; do not send recovery messages to real people or attempt password guessing.
acceptanceCriteria: Each finding identifies the intended authority transition and observed result.
No real credentials, OTPs, session values or identity documents are collected.
A role/session change is retested at the server boundary, not only in the UI.

questions.prompt: A logout button disappears but the old dummy session still authorizes a private local read. What is the relevant finding?
choices: The page needs a different color
The expected server-side session invalidation failed
All authentication algorithms are broken
questions.answer: The expected server-side session invalidation failed
questions.explanation: The proof concerns a specific lifecycle/authority transition. A bounded description avoids unsupported broader claims.

questions.prompt: Why can recovery be weaker than normal sign-in?
questions.answer: It may grant the same account authority with fewer or different checks, so its assurance and revocation effects need separate review.
questions.explanation: Strong normal login does not compensate for an unexamined alternate path.

reviewPrompts: Which state transition changed authority, and where is that enforced?

modules.title: 05. Browser interpretation and cross-origin trust
modules.description: Assess browser-context assumptions with harmless markers and reversible local actions.

lessons.title: Distinguish reflection from executable browser interpretation
objectives: Trace reflected, stored and DOM output contexts.
Validate context-sensitive defenses without reading cookies or creating external callbacks.

topics.title: Browser boundaries
details: A visible reflected string is not automatically executable script.
HTML, attribute, URL and script contexts require different handling.

topics.title: Harmless proof
details: Use an inert unique marker first and inspect the resulting DOM context.
If execution confirmation is needed, use only the owned lab's benign indicator and restore its state.

video.locator: Week 3 Securing Software: reflected/stored XSS and character escapes. Learn the interpretation boundary without assigning harmful payloads.

reading.locator: Reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS; contexts and prevention. Distinguish observing reflection from demonstrating unsafe interpretation.

assignment.title: A harmless output-context comparison
instructions: Place a unique plain-text marker through search, saved-note and client-rendered paths in the owned local teaching fixture.
Inspect the DOM and sink context; if the selected built-in lab requires active proof, use only its harmless visual indicator, with no cookie access, network calls, file access or persistent changes.
Compare a safely encoded/text-rendered version and test that ordinary user text still displays correctly; reset stored markers afterward.
deliverables: Minimal proof, safe-control comparison and reset log
acceptanceCriteria: Reflection alone is not reported as confirmed script execution.
No credentials, callbacks, exfiltration or harmful/persistent payload is used.
The proposed fix matches the actual output context and preserves legitimate text.

questions.prompt: Your marker appears on a page. What must still be established before claiming XSS?
choices: Only that the text is visible
That the page has any JavaScript
Unsafe interpretation/execution in the relevant browser context
questions.answer: Unsafe interpretation/execution in the relevant browser context
questions.explanation: Safely rendered text can reflect user input without becoming executable. Context and behavior determine the finding.

questions.prompt: Why is one generic escaping function not appropriate for every output context?
questions.answer: HTML text, attributes, URLs and script contexts have different parsing rules and required safe APIs or encodings.
questions.explanation: A defense must match the boundary where the data are interpreted.

reviewPrompts: At which sink does data become a browser instruction?

lessons.title: Assess CSRF and CORS as different boundaries
objectives: Distinguish unintended authenticated actions from cross-origin response reading.
Test only reversible dummy actions across explicitly owned local origins.

topics.title: CSRF conditions
details: Automatically attached authority can accompany an unintended request.
State-changing operations need the appropriate server-validated defense.

topics.title: CORS scope
details: CORS affects browser sharing of responses.
A permissive header is not by itself proof of sensitive credentialed data exposure.

reading.locator: How does CSRF work? and prevention: identify required conditions before testing a reversible local action.

assignment.title: Intermediate evidence gate: browser-boundary findings
instructions: Use two declared local origins and one dummy user to test a reversible note preference change with present/absent valid anti-CSRF context.
Separately compare allowed and unapproved origins reading a synthetic response under the fixture's credential policy.
Assemble your input/file, owner/session and browser findings with negative controls, redaction and restoration evidence.
deliverables: Intermediate finding dossier with proof limits
acceptanceCriteria: The report separates action authorization from browser response-sharing policy.
Any claimed CORS issue shows actual relevant synthetic data visibility under stated credential conditions.
All state changes are reversible, authorized and restored; no real user is involved.

questions.prompt: Does a broad Access-Control-Allow-Origin header alone prove sensitive credentialed data exposure?
choices: Yes, regardless of response contents
No, the full credential, response and browser behavior must be evaluated
Yes, and it authorizes testing any origin
questions.answer: No, the full credential, response and browser behavior must be evaluated
questions.explanation: Header observations require context and an authorized behavioral check. A finding must show the material boundary failure, not only a suspicious configuration.

questions.prompt: Why can blocking response reading fail to prevent a CSRF-style action?
questions.answer: A state-changing request can sometimes be sent and acted on even when the browser does not expose its response to the initiating origin.
questions.explanation: Sending/authorizing an action and reading its response are distinct security questions.

reviewPrompts: Did the test demonstrate a change, a read, or merely a header?

modules.title: 06. API permissions and server-side request boundaries
modules.description: Trace authority across API fields and delegated requests using tightly bounded local fixtures.

lessons.title: Assess object/function authorization and writable fields
objectives: Distinguish object-level, function-level and property-level permission checks.
Verify bounded input/resource limits without stress or denial-of-service testing.

topics.title: API authority
details: A caller may read a property without permission to write it.
Unexpected fields must not become privileged state automatically.

topics.title: Bounded testing
details: Use a documented local endpoint inventory rather than guessing public APIs.
Check limit boundaries with tiny requests and explicit budgets.

reading.locator: API documentation, supported methods/content types, hidden parameters and mass-assignment vulnerabilities. Apply only to the predeclared local schema.

assignment.title: A property-level permission challenge
instructions: Use a local synthetic user-profile API with declared editable displayName and server-controlled role/owner properties.
Within a five-request budget, compare valid edits, an unexpected property, a different known owner, a forbidden function and one tiny over-limit input.
Record whether unauthorized fields change durable state, then reset. Do not create load, discover real endpoints or acquire real privileges.
deliverables: Five bounded test records with state verification
acceptanceCriteria: The finding distinguishes rejected input, ignored fields and actual unauthorized state changes.
Allowed user edits still work as a positive control.
No performance degradation, resource exhaustion or non-lab request occurs.

questions.prompt: An API returns a user's role. Does that imply the user may set that role?
choices: Yes, every returned property is writable
No, read and write permissions differ
Yes, if the UI hides the field
questions.answer: No, read and write permissions differ
questions.explanation: Property-level authorization must distinguish disclosure from modification. Serialization output is not a grant of write authority.

questions.prompt: Why inspect stored state after a suspicious API response?
questions.answer: A response may echo input without applying it, or may hide a write despite an error; durable state confirms the actual effect.
questions.explanation: Findings should describe observed authority changes, not infer them from presentation alone.

reviewPrompts: Which property is authoritative, and who is allowed to change it?

lessons.title: Validate delegated fetch boundaries with local sinks
objectives: Explain how a user-controlled destination can borrow server authority.
Prove a destination-validation failure without contacting sensitive services.

topics.title: SSRF mechanism
details: A server fetch can cross a boundary the client itself could not cross.
Redirects, name resolution and protocol choices affect destination policy.

topics.title: Safe confirmation
details: Two expressly owned local sinks can show an allowed-versus-denied destination difference.
Never use cloud metadata, private-network discovery or an external callback as proof.

reading.locator: What is SSRF?, common attack surfaces and defenses; translate the mechanism into the two-sink isolated exercise, excluding sensitive target examples.

assignment.title: A two-sink server-request proof
instructions: Within the approved isolated lab, create two harmless HTTP sinks: A explicitly allowed by the fixture policy and B explicitly forbidden but still owned and authorized for this test.
Submit a unique non-secret marker through the local fetch feature and observe which sink receives it; optionally use one local-only redirect between these same sinks to test policy revalidation.
Document and fix destination enforcement, then retest. Never query cloud metadata, host services, unknown addresses, other protocols or external collectors.
acceptanceCriteria: All requests stay among the three declared local components.
A finding is supported by a sink observation, not just a timeout or error message.
The corrected policy validates the actual destination at the relevant boundary, including an allowed local redirect test if used.

questions.prompt: Which proof is appropriate for this SSRF lesson?
choices: A harmless marker reaching an explicitly authorized but policy-forbidden local sink
Reading cloud instance credentials
Scanning unknown internal addresses
questions.answer: A harmless marker reaching an explicitly authorized but policy-forbidden local sink
questions.explanation: The local observation proves the destination-policy failure without expanding scope or collecting sensitive data.

questions.prompt: Why can validating only an initial URL be insufficient?
questions.answer: A subsequent redirect or resolved destination may differ from what the original check allowed, so enforcement must cover the actual request path under the declared policy.
questions.explanation: The trust boundary concerns where the server ultimately sends the request, not only the first string it receives.

reviewPrompts: Whose authority is performing this request, and which destination policy constrains it?

modules.title: 07. Local network, transport and container configuration assessment
modules.description: Review concrete exposure and privilege assumptions without exploit chains, host escape or unknown-target scanning.

lessons.title: Assess known service exposure and transport assumptions
objectives: Compare declared and effective local network reachability.
Evaluate transport protection with synthetic traffic and certificate checks.

topics.title: Exposure review
details: Published ports, host binding and segmentation jointly affect reachability.
Service banners can guide a review but do not prove an exploitable weakness.

topics.title: Transport evidence
details: Plaintext dummy traffic demonstrates a confidentiality boundary without real credentials.
TLS failures must not be bypassed to make a test pass.

video.locator: Week 2 Securing Systems: HTTP/HTTPS, certificates, VPN and firewalls. Use only declared local endpoints and benign traffic.

reading.locator: 02-Configuration_and_Deployment_Management_Testing and 09-Testing_for_Weak_Cryptography: configuration and transport review, with current TLS guidance replacing historical defaults.

assignment.title: A known-endpoint transport and reachability review
instructions: Use the declared client/app/database lab flow matrix and inspect published port bindings before any connection attempt.
Verify one allowed and one denied connection using harmless requests to those exact owned endpoints, never a scan range.
Compare a synthetic plaintext marker with a correctly validated local TLS connection, documenting why certificate failures are findings rather than reasons to disable verification.
acceptanceCriteria: Only listed endpoints are contacted and no real traffic is captured.
A version/banner alone is not labelled proof of exploitability.
A proposed fix preserves required access and enforces TLS validation and scope.

questions.prompt: An old-looking service banner alone supports which conclusion?
choices: A lead for version and exposure verification
A confirmed vulnerable deployment without checking its actual patched build
A high-confidence impact rating without reachability or configuration evidence
questions.answer: A lead for version and exposure verification
questions.explanation: Backports, configuration and actual reachability matter. Confirm the relevant condition within scope instead of assigning impact from a string.

questions.prompt: Why test legitimate connectivity after tightening a network policy?
questions.answer: A control that blocks required safe use may fail operational acceptance; both allowed and denied flows must match the intended policy.
questions.explanation: Security remediation must preserve the system's authorized function.

reviewPrompts: Does the evidence show reachability, weak protection or actual unauthorized access?

lessons.title: Review container privilege, mounts and build inputs
objectives: Explain how container settings affect host and workload boundaries.
Distinguish a risky configuration from proven impact without attempting escape.

topics.title: Runtime scope
details: Host mounts, privileged mode, user identity and published ports require justification.
A container is not automatically a complete security boundary.

topics.title: Build trust
details: Pinned base images, dependency inventory and provenance aid assessment.
A secret in a fictional image recipe should be replaced by a dummy handle, not collected from a real image.

reading.locator: 02-Configuration_and_Deployment_Management_Testing: deployment and infrastructure configuration review. Pair with the SLSA build-track definitions for provenance scope.

assignment.title: An offline container-boundary challenge
instructions: Author two synthetic container/configuration manifests: one unnecessarily privileged with an invented host-mount path, one least-privilege and loopback-bound.
Review capabilities, writable mounts, runtime user, base/dependency pinning and dummy-secret handling without launching the unsafe variant.
Propose a corrected manifest and tests that inspect configuration and expected access; do not attempt host escape, persistence or discovery of real secrets.
acceptanceCriteria: The unsafe example is reviewed offline and never applied to the host.
Impact claims state required conditions and affected boundaries.
Corrections remove unnecessary authority while retaining the declared local service function.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate way to assess a deliberately unsafe privileged-container example here?
choices: Run the unsafe example first and confirm containment afterward
Treat containerization alone as sufficient without reviewing mounts and privileges
Review the synthetic manifest offline and validate a safe corrected design
questions.answer: Review the synthetic manifest offline and validate a safe corrected design
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches configuration and authority reasoning without creating a dangerous host exposure or collecting real secrets.

questions.prompt: Why can a read-only host mount still be sensitive?
questions.answer: Read access can disclose private data or credentials even when modification is prevented.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality and integrity risks need separate evaluation; read-only is not synonymous with harmless.

reviewPrompts: What exact capability makes the configuration risky?

modules.title: 08. Tool validation, impact and prioritization
modules.description: Turn leads into minimally proven findings and prioritize them by actual context.

lessons.title: Challenge tool output with independent local checks
objectives: Treat proxy/scanner observations as hypotheses requiring validation.
Reproduce a bounded result without relying on a tool's severity label.

topics.title: Tool discipline
details: Tools need explicit target scope, rate budgets and logging.
Passive inspection and a few manual requests often answer a small lab question.

topics.title: False positives
details: Missing headers, banners and errors do not automatically establish material harm.
A clean tool result does not establish absence of weaknesses.

reading.locator: The Web Security Testing Framework: before/during/after development and maintenance phases; follow its Introduction cross-reference for balanced automated, manual and source-review methods.

assignment.title: A three-lead validation notebook
instructions: Use three prepared synthetic leads: a suspicious header, a query error and an owner-boundary observation from earlier lessons.
Confirm or reject each with a bounded manual local request or source/configuration check and a negative control; no automated broad scan is required.
Record tool/version/scope and why its initial label was insufficient. Free developer tools and a local HTTP client satisfy the route.
acceptanceCriteria: At least one unsupported lead is explicitly rejected or left unconfirmed.
Confirmed findings have a mechanism and actual scoped effect.
Tool output never substitutes for authorization or expands the request budget.

questions.prompt: A scanner labels a missing header critical. What should follow?
choices: Contextual validation of the actual risk and applicability
Automatic acceptance of the severity
Unapproved wider scanning
questions.answer: Contextual validation of the actual risk and applicability
questions.explanation: Tool labels lack the full business and architectural context. A report must justify the control expectation and demonstrated impact.

questions.prompt: Why record a rejected false positive?
questions.answer: It shows the assessment's reasoning and prevents repeated investigation or misleading inclusion in later summaries.
questions.explanation: Evidence discipline includes why a claim was not established.

reviewPrompts: Could another assessor reproduce the finding without your tool's label?

lessons.title: Rate impact, prerequisites and uncertainty responsibly
objectives: Separate technical severity, business consequence and confidence.
Describe a possible failure chain without executing additional harmful steps.

topics.title: Prioritization
details: Required privileges, reachable assets and data sensitivity affect impact.
A score is a structured estimate, not a substitute for a narrative.

topics.title: Confidence
details: Observed minimal proof and hypothesized wider impact must be distinguished.
Uncertainty can justify further authorized investigation, not an exaggerated claim.

reading.locator: Reporting guidance on risk, technical detail and remediation. Use the guide's structure while stating the current scope and uncertainty of every impact claim.

assignment.title: Advanced evidence gate: context-rated findings
instructions: Prioritize four synthetic findings from the web/API/configuration exercises by prerequisites, exposure, potential consequence, ease of remediation and evidence confidence.
For one hypothetical combined failure, draw the causal chain on paper and mark untested links; do not execute an escalation or collect more data.
Include the API/server-request matrix and offline container review, identifying what remains unconfirmed.
deliverables: Ranked finding register with confidence and rationale
Advanced assessment dossier and bounded impact diagram
acceptanceCriteria: Observed facts and hypothetical consequences are explicitly separated.
Each priority has a context-based reason, not only a tool score.
No chain validation goes beyond the existing authorization or minimal synthetic proof.

questions.prompt: A potentially severe issue has only a partial local proof. Which pair must remain distinct in the report?
choices: A single combined score treating suspected impact as confirmed
The tool's highest severity label used as the final decision
Potential impact and confidence in the evidence
questions.answer: Potential impact and confidence in the evidence
questions.explanation: A high-impact scenario can be weakly evidenced, while a modest issue may be certain. The distinction guides responsible prioritization.

questions.prompt: How should an untested step in a possible vulnerability chain be described?
questions.answer: As a hypothesis with stated prerequisites and uncertainty, not as a demonstrated compromise.
questions.explanation: A professional report does not turn a plausible narrative into claimed observation.

reviewPrompts: What would change this finding's priority without changing its underlying defect?

modules.title: 09. Controlled assessment, remediation and retesting
modules.description: Manage the engagement as an accountable change-and-evidence process rather than a list of tricks.

lessons.title: Run a time-bounded assessment with change control
objectives: Translate scope into test order, budgets and checkpoints.
Handle unexpected results and scope changes without silently continuing.

topics.title: Execution governance
details: Authorization, target version and fixture identity accompany each test.
Changes to scope or methods require explicit approval from the owner role.

topics.title: Operational discipline
details: Pause on unexplained errors or impact.
A completed assessment can contain untested items with honest reasons.

reading.locator: Assessment planning, execution and post-assessment activities in SP 800-115. Keep the historical process reference separate from current tool and protocol choices.

assignment.title: An assessment runbook with a stop drill
instructions: Plan a two-hour local assessment using a prioritized subset of the known fixture tests and a fixed request/evidence budget.
Include checkpoints for target health, scope and reset, plus a simulated unexpected-data inject that requires stopping.
Record tested, untested, blocked and not-applicable cases with distinct meanings; do not mark coverage complete by default.
acceptanceCriteria: Every test has a destination, expected boundary, proof limit and reset step.
The unexpected-data inject stops the affected work and records a scope decision.
Untested cases remain visible instead of being counted as passes.

questions.prompt: Time runs out before a planned test. How should it be reported?
choices: Passed because no problem was observed
Untested, with its scope and reason retained
Deleted from the plan without explanation
questions.answer: Untested, with its scope and reason retained
questions.explanation: Absence of testing is not evidence of protection. Coverage must distinguish a successful test from no test.

questions.prompt: What must accompany approval of a scope change?
questions.answer: The approving owner, exact new assets/actions, limits, timing and revised evidence/stop conditions.
questions.explanation: A vague instruction to continue cannot replace specific authorization.

reviewPrompts: Which result would require pausing the rest of the assessment?

lessons.title: Propose fixes at the failed enforcement boundary
objectives: Identify root causes rather than suppressing a proof string.
Choose fixes that preserve legitimate application behavior.

topics.title: Root cause
details: An input pattern is not the vulnerability; the failed interpretation or permission boundary is.
A compensating control may reduce risk without removing the root cause.

topics.title: Fix design
details: Parameterized queries, owner checks and destination policy address different mechanisms.
Changes require owner approval and a rollback plan even in a lab engagement.

reading.locator: Existing ASVS 5.0.0 PDF: V1 Encoding and Sanitization, V8 Authorization and relevant V4 API/Web Service requirements. Select exact IDs that address your confirmed finding.

assignment.title: A finding-to-control remediation patch
instructions: Choose one confirmed local input-boundary issue and one owner/API policy issue, using your own minimal fixture source rather than modifying third-party production code.
Apply owner-approved fixes at the authoritative boundary and add positive tests for legitimate input and owner actions.
Document any temporary compensating control, its limitations and expiry; retain before/after versions for retesting.
deliverables: Two scoped local fixes and regression tests
acceptanceCriteria: The fix addresses the mechanism, not just the exact test string.
Legitimate behavior remains supported.
Changed assumptions, rollback and remaining risk are documented.

questions.prompt: Blocking one quote character is a weak substitute for which SQL defense?
choices: Client-side character checks that the server does not enforce
Suppressing database errors without changing query construction
Correct parameter binding at the query boundary
questions.answer: Correct parameter binding at the query boundary
questions.explanation: The root issue is interpreting input as query syntax. Hiding a symptom or banning one character does not establish correct separation.

questions.prompt: Why label a compensating control differently from a root-cause fix?
questions.answer: It may reduce exposure or impact while the underlying defect remains, so its assumptions, limitations and expiry need explicit management.
questions.explanation: Risk reduction should not be misrepresented as complete remediation.

reviewPrompts: Which invariant now prevents the entire failure class?

lessons.title: Retest fixes and detect functional regressions
objectives: Reproduce the original bounded proof against the corrected version.
Test nearby cases and legitimate workflows without expanding scope.

topics.title: Retest contract
details: Record the fixed version and unchanged fixture assumptions.
A different status code alone may not prove that unauthorized state change stopped.

topics.title: Regression
details: Expected allowed behavior must still work.
A reopened finding retains its history and current owner.

video.locator: CS50P Week 5 - Unit Tests: regression and boundary cases; apply the pattern to your own local remediation tests.

reading.locator: Testing during maintenance and operations; use a repeatable regression/verification cycle after changes.

assignment.title: A defensible remediation retest
instructions: Rerun the original minimal proofs from l20 on the fixed local fixture with newly issued dummy sessions.
Check durable state, a nearby bounded variation and legitimate owner/quoted-text behavior.
Classify each finding fixed, partially mitigated, not fixed or unable to verify, with exact evidence and any revised scope limitation.
acceptanceCriteria: Closure requires the original boundary violation to stop, not merely an altered response.
At least one positive legitimate workflow is preserved for each fix.
Partial or unverifiable outcomes remain explicit and are not silently closed.

questions.prompt: The response now says forbidden, but an unauthorized dummy-record write still occurs. Is the finding fixed?
choices: Yes, the status code changed
Yes, if the UI hides the result
No, the protected state still changes
questions.answer: No, the protected state still changes
questions.explanation: The authoritative effect is the security property being tested. Presentation cannot substitute for enforcement.

questions.prompt: Why repeat tests with a fresh session after a fix?
questions.answer: It separates the corrected behavior from stale caches, old tokens or leftover fixture state that could give misleading results.
questions.explanation: Reproducibility includes identity and state setup, not only request text.

reviewPrompts: What exact observation justifies closing this finding?

modules.title: 10. Reporting, capstone and responsible handover
modules.description: Deliver a scoped assessment that a defender can reproduce, fix and operate safely.

lessons.title: Write executive and technical reports with bounded claims
objectives: Communicate business impact without overstating technical proof.
Give defenders sufficient reproduction and remediation detail without distributing sensitive data.

topics.title: Report audiences
details: Executives need scope, material risks and priorities.
Implementers need exact versions, preconditions, expected/actual behavior and verification steps.

topics.title: Safe reporting
details: Redact secrets and minimize synthetic record content.
State exclusions, untested areas and limitations prominently.

reading.locator: Reporting README: executive summary, scope, technical findings and remediation communication. Use your own wording and synthetic evidence.

assignment.title: A report that a defender can act on
instructions: Write an executive summary and two full technical findings from the local assessment, including one corrected finding.
For each, link minimal redacted evidence, prerequisites, confidence, impact, root cause, fix and retest status.
Include coverage/exclusions and a contrary interpretation you ruled out; do not publish real target details or contact external parties.
acceptanceCriteria: A reviewer can reproduce each finding using only the isolated fixture instructions.
Severity, confidence and observed effect are not conflated.
No credential, real personal information, unsupported compromise claim or certification claim appears.

questions.prompt: Which report title best matches one confirmed cross-owner dummy-note read?
choices: Critical account takeover inferred solely from one synthetic record read
Owner authorization missing on the scoped note-read operation
All tenant data are exposed without testing the relevant endpoints
questions.answer: Owner authorization missing on the scoped note-read operation
questions.explanation: A precise title identifies the actual enforcement failure and avoids unsupported broader impact claims.

questions.prompt: Why keep assessment exclusions in the executive summary?
questions.answer: Decision-makers may otherwise interpret limited testing as broad assurance over systems or risks that were never evaluated.
questions.explanation: Scope is essential context for every conclusion, not a minor appendix.

reviewPrompts: Could a defender fix and verify the issue without asking what you actually tested?

lessons.title: Deliver an authorized local assessment and verified remediation
objectives: Execute the complete assessment lifecycle on a declared disposable target.
Demonstrate minimal proof, root-cause fixes and independent retest evidence.

topics.title: Capstone scope
details: Use a local deliberately vulnerable teaching app plus owned minimal fixtures where code changes are needed.
Do not replace bounded proof with maximum exploitation or real-target activity.

topics.title: Evidence standard
details: A false positive rejected with evidence is useful work.
Readiness depends on scope, quality and remediation evidence, not finding count or severity inflation.

reading.locator: Use the v4.2 category folders matching your declared input, authorization, session/browser and API tests; cite exact versioned case IDs where applicable, paired with current PortSwigger/OWASP guidance.

assignment.title: Capstone: a scoped lab assessment defenders can reproduce
instructions: Define and sign off a rules-of-engagement pack for one pinned, isolated local training target and synthetic fixtures; verify containment/reset before testing.

Assess three distinct boundary types chosen from input/file interpretation, identity/ownership/session, browser trust and API/server requests. Use deliberately flawed local examples so confirming or rejecting the expected issue is assessable.
Produce minimal harmless proofs and at least one rejected false positive; implement root-cause fixes in your own fixture code and retest with positive/negative controls.

Deliver a redacted report, coverage register, residual-risk decisions and clean handover. Never use real accounts, unknown endpoints, credential harvesting, persistence/evasion, malware or harmful payloads.
deliverables: Authorization, scope, containment and reset evidence
Versioned synthetic fixture pack and bounded test log
Technical/executive report with minimal proofs and false-positive analysis
Remediation diffs and independent before/after retests
Residual-risk register, operations handover and teardown record
acceptanceCriteria: Every test stays within the expressly authorized isolated scope and stated request/data limits.
Three distinct mechanisms have a confirmed or correctly rejected finding supported by expected/actual behavior and controls.
No finding depends on real data extraction, external callbacks, covert access or destructive effects.
Fixes address enforcement mechanisms and preserve legitimate behavior.
A peer or delayed blind self-review reproduces selected findings and retests from the provided setup.
Untested areas, uncertainty and remaining risk are explicit.
The report makes no certification, job-readiness guarantee or authorization for real-world targets.

questions.prompt: Which result can satisfy this capstone's assessment standard?
choices: A bounded reproducible finding, a justified rejection and a verified fix
A high finding count with no evidence
An unauthorized real-target compromise
questions.answer: A bounded reproducible finding, a justified rejection and a verified fix
questions.explanation: The goal is authorized, useful and defensible assessment practice, not maximizing harm or inflating the number of findings.

questions.prompt: Why does finishing this capstone not authorize testing a real organization?
questions.answer: Authorization is granted by the owner for specific assets and actions; educational completion creates neither that permission nor a professional certification.
questions.explanation: Skill and permission are separate. Every real engagement needs its own explicit scope and safeguards.

reviewPrompts: Can a reviewer establish the finding and the fix without trusting an unexplained screenshot?

lessons.title: Practice responsible disclosure and close the engagement
objectives: Communicate a finding through an agreed owner channel without public pressure or unnecessary disclosure.
Close or transfer remaining risks and remove lab artifacts safely.

topics.title: Responsible disclosure
details: Use the owner's published policy and agreed scope; do not promise universal legal protection.
Coordinate evidence access, remediation and publication decisions with the authorized owner.

topics.title: Closure
details: Finding status, residual risk and retest limitations remain visible.
Destroy disposable secrets and restore only explicitly owned lab resources.

reading.locator: Reporting and final communication guidance; pair with SP 800-115 post-assessment activities for remediation and final deliverables.

assignment.title: A fictional disclosure and closure tabletop
instructions: Draft a private disclosure to the fictional lab owner with scope, minimal proof, impact confidence and a proposed remediation/retest process; do not send it to a real vendor.
Role-play acknowledgement, a disputed finding and a partial fix, recording evidence-based resolutions and unverified status.
Hand over the final report, remove dummy credentials/interception profiles, reset the target and verify that no vulnerable listener remains outside the declared retained lab.
deliverables: Final finding register and residual-risk handover
acceptanceCriteria: No real third party is contacted or pressured and no real vulnerability is publicly disclosed.
Disputed or partial findings remain accurately labelled with next steps.
Only known lab resources are cleaned up; real browser/Auth data, host settings and other services are untouched.

questions.prompt: An owner disputes a finding. What is the professional next step?
choices: Keep the original severity without addressing the owner's counterexample
Clarify the scoped evidence and reproduce or revise the claim
Close solely because the owner disagrees, without a verification record
questions.answer: Clarify the scoped evidence and reproduce or revise the claim
questions.explanation: Responsible communication is evidence-led and permission-bound. Disagreement does not authorize pressure, disclosure of secrets or expanded access.

questions.prompt: What should remain after the lab itself is removed?
questions.answer: A minimal redacted evidence/report package under the agreed retention policy, with scope, versions, findings, remediation status and residual-risk owners.
questions.explanation: Safe closure preserves useful learning and accountability without retaining unnecessary sensitive or dangerous artifacts.

reviewPrompts: What permission, evidence and responsibility remain at engagement closure?

sources.title: PortSwigger free Web Security Academy
sources.notes: Public topic readings; optional assigned hosted labs may require a free account. No paid tool or certificate is required.

sources.title: OWASP WSTG version 4.2 official source
sources.notes: Versioned source used instead of the currently broken stable redirect; named framework/testing/reporting directories verified.

sources.title: OWASP Juice Shop official project
sources.notes: Local isolated training target only, never the shared public demo.

sources.title: OWASP WebGoat official README and safety warnings
sources.notes: Explicit local binding and isolation guidance; dummy local accounts only.

sources.title: NIST technical assessment process
sources.notes: 2008 historical framework, complemented by modern web/security guidance.

sources.title: CMU CyLab Security Academy
sources.notes: Current migrated picoCTF learning platform, optional free-account practice within assigned CTF rules.

limitations: Ethical Hacking means expressly authorized assessment in owned, isolated local labs or provider-assigned CTF instances, with synthetic data and minimal harmless proof. No real-target intrusion, real credential/personal-data collection, covert access, persistence/evasion, malware, harmful payloads or unapproved scanning.

Professional Practice is a learning level, not certification, qualification, guaranteed job mastery or permission to test real organizations. Computer Security Systems explains protections; this topic assesses bounded failure conditions and verifies fixes.

The core route uses free public readings, free local tools and owned synthetic fixtures. PortSwigger and CMU hosted practice are optional and may require free accounts; provider authorization never extends to unrelated infrastructure.

Deliberately vulnerable applications must remain loopback/host-only, disposable and separated from real accounts, data, host mounts and production networks. Pin supported official releases, verify reset and stop if containment is uncertain.

Do not run test tooling against any real target while following the examples. Minimize proof, avoid destructive/resource-exhausting actions and use only the declared request budget, local sinks and marker files.

WSTG v4.2 and NIST SP 800-115 provide versioned/historical process references. Current defensive standards and official maintained tool documentation govern contemporary configuration; no historical technique creates present-day legal authorization.
Shared Common Foundation/SDE/Computer Security Systems prerequisites and the existing ASVS PDF keep canonical IDs and checksums. No book, solution, video or new PDF is copied or rehosted.
